q: A Service `api` exists, but `curl api` from another pod fails. `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api` shows no addresses. What should you check first?
options: Whether the Service selector matches the pods' labels and whether those pods are Ready
CoreDNS logs
kube-proxy mode
The node's firewall
explain: Empty endpoints mean no Ready pod matches the selector. DNS and kube-proxy are working as designed; they have nothing to route to. Compare `kubectl get svc api -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector}'` with `kubectl get pods --show-labels` and check readiness.

q: Endpoints exist and point to the right pods, but connections to the Service are refused. `kubectl exec` into the pod and `curl localhost:3000` works. What are the two most likely causes?
options: Wrong namespace or DNS search domain
The pod's QoS class is BestEffort
sessionAffinity is enabled
`targetPort` does not match the listening port, or the app binds to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0
explain: Traffic arrives at podIP:targetPort. If the process listens on a different port, or only on loopback, other pods are refused even though localhost works inside the pod.

q: Which statements about the Kubernetes network model are true? (select all)
options: Every pod gets its own IP address
Pods on different nodes can reach each other's IPs without NAT
Containers in the same pod each get a different IP
The CNI plugin is responsible for pod networking
explain: The model requires one IP per pod (shared by its containers) and flat pod-to-pod connectivity across nodes. Kubernetes delegates the implementation to a CNI plugin such as kindnet, VPC CNI, Calico or Cilium.

q: A Service has `port: 80`, `targetPort: http`, `nodePort: 30080`, `type: NodePort`. The pod's container declares `ports: [{name: http, containerPort: 3000}]`. Which is correct?
options: In-cluster clients use `svc:3000`; external clients use `node:80`
In-cluster clients use `svc:80`; external clients use `<node-ip>:30080`; traffic reaches the pod on 3000
Everyone uses port 30080
The Service is invalid because targetPort must be a number
explain: `port` is the ClusterIP port, `nodePort` is opened on every node, and `targetPort` (here the named port `http` → 3000) is where the pod listens.

q: Which Service type returns the individual pod IPs from DNS instead of a single virtual IP?
options: Headless (`clusterIP: None`)
ClusterIP
NodePort
ExternalName
explain: A headless Service has no ClusterIP and no kube-proxy rules; CoreDNS returns an A record per Ready endpoint, and StatefulSet pods get per-pod names.

q: You set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on a NodePort Service. Requests to node A time out, while node B works. Why?
options: Node A's kube-proxy crashed
Local disables NodePorts on control-plane nodes
Node A runs no pod for that Service; with Local, nodes only forward to local endpoints
Session affinity is required with Local
explain: `Local` preserves the client source IP and avoids an extra hop, but a node without a local endpoint drops the traffic. Cloud load balancers health-check nodes to send traffic only to those with endpoints.

q: From a pod in namespace `shop`, which name resolves to Service `redis` in namespace `cache`?
options: `redis`
`redis.cache`
`cache.redis`
`redis.shop.cache`
explain: The search list includes `svc.cluster.local`, so `redis.cache` expands to `redis.cache.svc.cluster.local`. Plain `redis` would look in the caller's namespace first (`redis.shop.svc.cluster.local`).

q: Your Node.js service calls `api.stripe.com` thousands of times per minute and CoreDNS CPU is high. What is the main cause and a fix?
options: Stripe's DNS is slow; switch providers
CoreDNS does not cache external names; install Redis
Pods cannot resolve external names; use hostNetwork
`ndots:5` makes each lookup try the cluster search domains first (several NXDOMAIN queries); use `api.stripe.com.` or lower `ndots` via `dnsConfig`, and reuse connections
explain: Names with fewer than 5 dots are tried with each search domain before as-is, for A and AAAA. A trailing dot or `ndots: "2"` cuts that; keep-alive agents reduce lookups; NodeLocal DNSCache helps at scale.

q: Which statements about kube-proxy are true? (select all)
options: In iptables mode it chooses a backend per connection using random-probability rules
It proxies every packet through a user-space process
nftables mode is stable and is the successor to iptables mode
IPVS mode is deprecated in recent Kubernetes versions
explain: kube-proxy programs kernel rules; traffic does not flow through kube-proxy itself. nftables mode is stable since v1.33, and IPVS mode was deprecated in v1.35.

q: You scale a gRPC backend from 2 to 10 pods, but CPU stays high on the original 2 and the new ones are idle. Why?
options: New pods are not Ready
gRPC is UDP-based and not supported by Services
kube-proxy balances per connection; long-lived HTTP/2 connections stay on the original pods
The Service needs `sessionAffinity: None`
explain: ClusterIP load balancing happens when a connection is established. gRPC multiplexes many requests over one long-lived connection, so it does not rebalance. Use client-side balancing with a headless Service, connection max-age, or an L7 proxy/mesh.

q: On a fresh kind cluster, a `type: LoadBalancer` Service shows `EXTERNAL-IP <pending>` forever. Why?
options: No controller provisions load balancers; run cloud-provider-kind (or MetalLB)
kind does not support Services
LoadBalancer requires `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`
The Service needs an Ingress
explain: Kubernetes only allocates the ClusterIP and NodePort; a cloud controller must create the actual LB and write its address. cloud-provider-kind plays that role locally (on macOS run it with sudo and `--enable-lb-port-mapping`).

q: You create an ExternalName Service `docs` pointing to `kubernetes.io`. `dig docs` shows the CNAME, but `curl https://docs` fails. Why?
options: ExternalName only works for UDP
CoreDNS blocks external CNAMEs
ExternalName requires a selector
ExternalName is a pure DNS alias; the client still sends `docs` as Host/SNI, so the remote server's certificate and virtual hosts do not match
explain: No proxying or header rewriting happens. ExternalName works best for protocols that ignore the hostname or servers configured to accept the alias.

q: During graceful termination, what does a pod's EndpointSlice entry look like?
options: It is deleted immediately
`ready: false`, `serving: true` (if readiness still passes), `terminating: true`
`ready: true` until SIGKILL
It moves to a separate terminating Service
explain: The endpoint remains with conditions that let kube-proxy stop sending new connections while existing ones drain. `serving` reflects readiness regardless of termination.
